open-question.question: The live verification mixes runner-executed checks (the plugin install and two headless agent dispatches) with one check the maintainer must run by hand in an interactive session, and a headless complete-all-tasks run has no one to pause for. How is the maintainer's interactive check placed relative to the task list?
open-question.recommendation: The whole verification is derived into the initial batch, so the maintainer's check is listed in TASKS_TODO.md and no clean end-of-run report can hide it. The three runner outcomes are committed at a task boundary before the pause, so the dispatches never run twice and a quota stop resumes from committed state. A FAILED at that task is accurate, not a disguise: the task's bar is unmet until the maintainer has run the check, and the commit the inline skill leaves in the workspace is the evidence the second run reads.
open-question.alternative: The interactive check is its own task, the last one in the initial batch. It comes right after a runner verification task that does the plugin install and the two headless agent dispatches, records those three outcomes in TASKS_DONE.md, and keeps the temporary workspace. The brief of the interactive-check task says it passes only when the workspace shows that the maintainer ran the inline skill interactively, such as the commit that skill leaves in the workspace's git history. It also says the completer must never run the skill itself. A headless complete-all-tasks agent finds no such evidence and returns FAILED, so the loop stops there. The maintainer then runs the check by hand in an interactive Codex session and runs the task again with complete-task or complete-all-tasks. That run checks the workspace evidence, records the fourth outcome, and deletes the workspace. derive-tasks writes the whole verification into the initial batch, so the maintainer's step is listed in TASKS_TODO.md and can't be forgotten. The pause lands exactly between the runner's checks and the maintainer's. Because the dispatches sit in an already-completed task, they are never run twice, which keeps the "each still runs exactly once" rule and the free-tier quota safe. It uses FAILED as a planned pause, so the run reports a real failure for an expected stop, and nothing in the report tells the two apart. The headless agent might also try to produce the evidence itself, for example by running the skill through codex exec, which would break the split between modes and spend a scarce model call. Only the brief's wording prevents that. Using a commit in the workspace as evidence works only if the chosen inline skill commits anything, and the sibling question "Verification inline skill" decides which skill that is.

All four checks sit in one verification task, the last one in the initial batch. The headless complete-all-tasks agent does the install and both headless dispatches. When it reaches the interactive check it returns FAILED, leaving the three outcomes as resumable partial work: uncommitted changes in the cairn tree plus the kept temporary workspace. The maintainer runs the interactive check by hand. A second run of the same task picks up the partial work, adds the maintainer's check from the workspace evidence, and writes all four outcomes as one TASKS_DONE.md entry. All four outcomes land in one TASKS_DONE.md entry under one Task-completion commit, which matches the run-mode decision's "records all four outcomes" in the simplest shape. The task list also stays one task shorter. Between the two runs, the three runner outcomes exist only as uncommitted partial work. If the resumed completer misreads them, it runs the dispatches again, spending the scarce free-tier quota and breaking "each still runs exactly once". The quota-exhaustion rule of "pick up at the first unrun check" then depends on reading that partial state, not on committed task boundaries. It shares the FAILED-as-pause cost, and the commit-evidence condition on the sibling question "Verification inline skill", with the designed-stop option.

The initial batch ends with the runner verification task: install plus the two headless dispatches, with the three outcomes recorded in TASKS_DONE.md and the temporary workspace kept. The interactive check is in no task. The maintainer runs it by hand after complete-all-tasks finishes cleanly. A follow-up task is then added through submit-task. It records the fourth outcome, checked against the workspace's evidence plus the maintainer's observation written into its brief, and deletes the workspace. This is the same after-the-batch follow-up path the contradiction-handling decision already uses. No task is designed to fail, the headless run ends on its normal success line, and every task in the batch can be done fully unattended. The maintainer's step reuses an existing path, follow-up tasks via submit-task, so no new convention is needed. The maintainer's step appears nowhere in TASKS_TODO.md, so only the maintainer's memory of the milestone keeps it from being skipped. "All tasks completed." is printed while one required check hasn't run. The follow-up task is written after the fact by the person whose check it records, not derived with the batch. Its evidence again depends on the inline skill leaving a trace in the workspace, and the sibling question "Verification inline skill" decides which skill that is.

The initial batch holds no verification task, and complete-all-tasks runs it headless to the end. Afterwards a single verification task is added through submit-task and completed inline with complete-task in an interactive cairn session. That runner does the install and runs both dispatches as headless codex exec runs. It then asks the maintainer to run the interactive Codex check, waits in the conversation for the result, confirms it against the workspace, and records all four outcomes in one TASKS_DONE.md entry. The check happens inside the task that records it, so no designed failure is needed, and all four outcomes still land in one entry. The runner can ask the maintainer directly and follow up on an unclear result in conversation instead of guessing from leftover files. The complete-task procedure has no step for waiting on a person, so the pause depends on the inline runner choosing to ask. The same task run through complete-all-tasks would have no one to ask. The verification is missing from the derived batch, so its existence again depends on the maintainer remembering to submit it. A long single task that waits on a person also has no committed checkpoint if the quota runs out partway.

This rejects the premise of a headless run. The whole task list, including a final verification task that holds all four checks, is completed by the maintainer with complete-task, one task at a time, in an interactive cairn session. complete-all-tasks is not used for this milestone. When the verification task reaches the interactive check, the runner pauses for the maintainer, takes the outcome from the conversation and the workspace, and records all four in one entry. Every task, the verification included, is derived into the initial batch and run by someone who can be asked. No task fails by design and none is added later. It gives up unattended completion for the whole milestone just to handle one step. The maintainer has to drive every task of a long batch by hand. Nothing in the list stops a later complete-all-tasks call from reaching the verification task headless, where it has no one to ask.
